slides.title: Page Replacement Basics
slides.body: Page Replacement Basics
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Page Replacement Basics

slides.title: Why Replacement Needed
slides.body:
Frames Are Finite
Demand paging loads pages only when referenced
Every running process competes for the same limited frames
Allocated frames eventually all hold valid pages
A newly needed page must then displace an existing one
Physical memory offers only a limited number of frames, so a new page fault cannot always find an empty frame to occupy
slides.notes: So, let's understand the need for Page Replacement. Since Physical Memory contains only a limited number of Frames, there comes a point whereall the available Frames are occupied. If a Page Fault occurs after that,the operating system cannot simply load the required page. Instead, it has to replace one of the existing Pages with the newly required page, and that's exactly why Page Replacement is needed.

slides.title: Trigger Condition
slides.body:
No Free Frame
Page fault occurs on an invalid or absent page
OS first checks the free-frame list
Free frame available: page loaded directly, no eviction
Free-frame list empty: a resident page must be evicted
Replacement is invoked only when a page fault occurs and the OS's free-frame list is empty
slides.notes: Now, let's see when Page Replacement actually gets triggered. It doesn't happen for every Page Fault. Whenever a Page Fault occurs, the operating system first checks its free-frame list. If a Free Frame is available, the required page is loaded directly. However, if the free-frame list is empty, the OS has no choice but to evict one of the resident Pages before loading the new one.

slides.title: Choosing Victim
slides.body:
Which Page Evicted
A page-replacement algorithm is the policy that decides which resident page becomes the victim when a frame must be reclaimed. Algorithms are judged by the page faults they cause on a reference string — the ordered sequence of page numbers a process accesses over time
slides.notes: Moving on, once Page Replacement is required, the next question is which Page should be removed. This decision is made by a Page-Replacement Algorithm, which selects the victim page from the resident pages. Different algorithms follow different strategies, and their performance is mainly compared based on the number of Page Faults they generate for a given Reference String.

slides.title: Choosing Victim
slides.body:
Which Page Evicted
Decides which frame is freed for the incoming page
Aim: minimise the future page-fault rate
Different policies trade prediction accuracy for bookkeeping overhead
Common policies: FIFO, Optimal, LRU, LFU/MFU
slides.notes: Next, let's understand how the victim page is selected. A Page-Replacement Algorithm decides which Frame should be freed so the incoming page can be loaded. The main objective is to minimise the number of future Page Faults, but different algorithms achieve this with different levels of tracking and overhead. Some of the commonly used policies are FIFO, Optimal, LRU, and LFU/MFU.

slides.title: Replacement Steps
slides.body:
Ordered Sequence
On a page fault, the OS runs a fixed sequence to bring in the required page, evicting a resident page only when no frame is free:
slides.notes: Now, let's walk through the initial Replacement Steps followed after a Page Fault. First, the CPU tries to access a page that is not present in memory, which triggers a Page Fault.  Control is then transferred to the operating system through a trap, allowing the page-fault handler to take over. Finally, the OS locates the required page on the backing store before proceeding with the replacement process.
tables: Page fault occurs - the CPU references a page not currently in memory
Trap to the OS - hardware interrupts, control passes to the page-fault handler
Locate the desired page on the backing store (disk)

slides.title: Replacement Steps
slides.body:
Ordered Sequence
On a page fault, the OS runs a fixed sequence to bring in the required page, evicting a resident page only when no frame is free:
slides.notes: Moving on, the OS now checks for a Free Frame. If one is available, it loads the required page directly; otherwise, a Page-Replacement Algorithm is used to select a victim frame. Before replacing it, the OS checks the dirty bit to determine whether the page needs to be written back to disk. Finally, the required page is loaded, the Page Table is updated, and the interrupted instruction is restarted.
tables: Find a free frame -  if one exists, use it and skip to Step 6; if none is free, apply the replacement algorithm to select a victim frame
If a victim was selected, check its dirty bit - write it back to disk if modified, else discard it
Load the desired page into the free frame; update the page table (and the victim's entry)
Restart the instruction that caused the fault

slides.title: Modified Bit Role
slides.body:
Reducing Write Cost
Dirty bit set the moment a page is written
Clean victim page: discard directly, no disk write
Dirty victim page: must write back before reuse
Avoiding unnecessary write-backs cuts replacement cost
Overall goal: minimise page-fault rate and total overhead
The dirty (modified) bit marks a page whose frame content differs from its backing-store copy, guiding whether a write-back is needed
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the Modified Bit, also known as the dirty bit. It is a status bit that indicates whether a page has been modified after being loaded into memory. If the page hasn't changed, it is considered clean and can be discarded directly during Page Replacement. However, if the dirty bit is set, the updated page must be written back to the disk, meaning the modified contents are saved to the backing store before the frame is reused. This avoids losing any changes while also preventing unnecessary disk writes, helping reduce the overall replacement cost.

slides.title: Policy Families
slides.body:
How Victims Are Chosen
Every page-replacement algorithm in this session falls into one of four families, differing only in the signal it uses to pick the victim page:
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at the different families of Page-Replacement Algorithms. Although each algorithm follows its own strategy, they can be grouped into four families based on the criterion they use to choose the victim page. FIFO-based algorithms evict pages based on their arrival order, Optimal chooses the page that will be used farthest in the future, Recency-based algorithms consider how recently a page was accessed, and Counting-based algorithms use the frequency of page references. We'll now understand each of these families and their algorithms in detail.

slides.title: FIFO & Optimal
slides.body: FIFO & Optimal
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the FIFO & Optimal

slides.title: FIFO Replacement
slides.body:
Oldest Page Evicted
Maintains a queue of resident pages in load order
New page enters at the rear of the queue
Fault with no free frame evicts the front (oldest) page
Simple to implement with a queue or circular pointer
Ignores whether the evicted page is still actively used
FIFO evicts the page that has resided in memory longest, treating resident frames as a simple arrival-ordered queue
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the FIFO (First-In, First-Out) Page Replacement algorithm. As the name suggests, it always removes the page that has been in memory for the longest time, regardless of how frequently it is being used. To achieve this, the operating system maintains the resident pages in a queue, where every new page is added at the rear. When a Page Fault occurs and no Free Frame is available, the page at the front of the queue is selected as the victim page. Since FIFO doesn't consider recent page usage, it may sometimes replace a page that is still actively needed.

slides.title: FIFO Key Drawback
slides.body:
Anomaly Preview
Extra frames are expected to reduce faults, not raise them
FIFO occasionally violates this expectation on certain reference strings
This counter-intuitive rise is named Belady's Anomaly
FIFO can behave counter-intuitively: adding more frames sometimes increases the fault count instead of decreasing it
slides.notes: Next, let's look at a major drawback of FIFO. Normally, we expect that increasing the number of Frames should reduce the number of Page Faults because more pages can stay in memory. However, FIFO doesn't always follow this expectation. For certain Reference Strings, adding more Frames can actually increase the number of Page Faults. This unexpected behaviour is known as Belady's Anomaly, which we'll understand in detail later.

slides.title: Optimal Replacement
slides.body:
Future Knowledge Ideal
Optimal replacement evicts the page that will not be referenced again for the longest time ahead, minimising faults for a given frame count
Requires complete knowledge of the future reference sequence
Victim chosen: page unused for the longest span ahead, or never again
Produces the fewest possible faults for any frame count
Not implementable in real systems since future references are unknown
Used purely as a theoretical benchmark for other algorithms
slides.notes: Moving on, let's understand the Optimal Replacement algorithm. It selects the victim page that will not be referenced again for the longest time in the future, or may never be used again. Since this choice is always the best possible, it produces the minimum number of Page Faults for a given number of Frames. However, implementing this algorithm in a real system is not practical because the operating system cannot predict future Reference Strings. That's why Optimal Replacement is mainly used as a theoretical benchmark to compare the performance of other Page-Replacement Algorithms.

slides.title: LRU & Approximations
slides.body: LRU & Approximations
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the LRU & Approximations

slides.title: Why LRU Works
slides.body:
Recency Predicts Reuse
Assumes recently accessed pages are likely accessed again soon
Contrasts with FIFO, which ignores usage after loading
Approaches Optimal fault count for many real workloads
Relies on temporal locality: recently used pages tend to be used again soon
LRU replaces the page that has gone unreferenced for the longest time, applying temporal locality to predict future access
slides.notes: Now, let's understand why the LRU (Least Recently Used) algorithm works so well. It is based on the principle of temporal locality, which assumes that if a page has been accessed recently, it is likely to be accessed again in the near future. So, instead of removing the oldest page like FIFO, LRU replaces the page that has not been used for the longest time. Because of this approach, LRU often achieves a Page Fault rate that is very close to the Optimal Replacement algorithm for many real-world workloads.

slides.title: LRU Implementation
slides.body:
Counter Or Stack
Exact LRU can be realised with a counter that timestamps every access or a stack that reorders pages on each reference
slides.notes: Moving on, let's see how LRU can be implemented in practice. One approach is the Counter-based method, where every page access is assigned a timestamp, and the page with the oldest timestamp is selected for replacement. Another approach is the Stack-based method, where every accessed page is moved to the top of a stack, making the page at the bottom the Least Recently Used page. While both methods accurately implement LRU, they require frequent updates to timestamps or stack pointers, making them expensive to maintain in real systems.
tables: Hardware clock timestamps every page on access; evict smallest timestamp
Requires searching timestamps and frequent updates
Accessed page moves to top of a doubly-linked list; evict bottom
Every reference forces list pointer updates

slides.title: LRU Implementation Cost
slides.body:
Overhead Too High
Counter method needs a clock update on every reference
Stack method needs list re-linking on every reference
Commodity CPUs provide no full-order LRU hardware
Operating systems use cheaper approximations instead of exact LRU
True LRU needs hardware or software bookkeeping on every single memory reference, making it impractical at real memory-access speeds
slides.notes: Now, although LRU gives good performance, implementing true LRU comes with a high cost. Every memory reference must be tracked, either by updating a Counter or by rearranging a Stack, which introduces significant bookkeeping overhead. Since most commodity CPUs do not provide hardware support for maintaining the exact LRU order, implementing it efficiently becomes difficult.Therefore, operating systems usually prefer approximations of LRU that offer similar performance with much lower overhead.

slides.title: Reference Bit Basics
slides.body:
Not Recently Used
Hardware sets reference bit to 1 on every page access
OS clears all reference bits at fixed intervals
Bit still 0 at fault time: page unused recently
Not-Recently-Used (NRU) evicts from the bit-0 group first
Far cheaper than counters, but coarser than true LRU
A single hardware reference bit, set on access and cleared periodically, cheaply approximates which pages saw recent use
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the Reference Bit. It is a hardware-maintained bit that helps the operating system identify whether a page was used recently, without maintaining the complete access history like LRU. The hardware sets the Reference Bit whenever a page is accessed, and the operating system clears it after fixed intervals to begin a new observation period. During Page Replacement, if a page's Reference Bit is still 0, it is considered Not Recently Used (NRU) and becomes a good candidate for replacement. This method is much simpler and has lower overhead than implementing true LRU.

slides.title: Second Chance Algo
slides.body:
Pages sit in a circular queue with a clock hand
Hand checks reference bit of the pointed page
Bit = 1: clear it, skip page, advance hand
Bit = 0: evict this page, insert new page here
Also called the Clock algorithm for its circular sweep
Clock Hand Sweep
Second chance augments FIFO with a reference bit: a page is evicted only if its bit is already clear when the clock hand reaches it
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Second Chance Algorithm, which is an improved version of FIFO. Instead of immediately replacing the oldest page, it first checks the page's Reference Bit. If the Reference Bit is 1, the page is given a second chance by clearing the bit and moving the clock hand to the next page. If the Reference Bit is 0, that page is selected as the victim page and replaced with the incoming page. Since the pages are arranged in a circular queue and the pointer moves in a circular manner, this approach is also known as the Clock Algorithm.

slides.title: Enhanced Second Chance
slides.body:
Reference And Modify
Enhanced second chance adds the modify bit, ranking pages into four classes so clean, unused pages are evicted before dirty ones
slides.notes: Moving on, the Enhanced Second Chance algorithm uses both the Reference Bit and the Modify Bit to choose the victim page. Here, 0 means the bit is not set, while 1 means it is set. So, (0,0) represents a page that is neither recently used nor modified, making it the best choice for replacement. As we move to (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1), the pages become less suitable because they are either modified, recently used, or both.

slides.title: MRU Replacement
slides.body:
Victim: the most recently accessed resident page
Inverts LRU's assumption that recent use predicts near reuse
Wins on cyclic or large sequential scans of data bigger than the frames
Loses badly on ordinary locality-heavy workloads
Rare in practice; mainly seen in database buffer managers
MRU evicts the page referenced most recently, the exact inverse of LRU, and helps only when a just-used page is the least likely to be needed again soon
Evict Most Recently Used
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the MRU (Most Recently Used) algorithm. Unlike LRU, MRU selects the page that was accessed most recently as the victim page. It works well in situations like large sequential or cyclic data scans, where a recently used page is less likely to be needed again soon. However, for most applications that exhibit locality, MRU performs poorly, which is why it is rarely used in general-purpose operating systems.

slides.title: Counting-Based (LFU / MFU)
slides.body: Counting-Based (LFU / MFU)
slides.notes:
Npw we will learn about the Counting-Based 
(LFU / MFU)

slides.title: Counting-Based Idea
slides.body:
Frequency As Signal
Every resident page carries a reference-count field
Count increments on each hit to that page
Two opposite policies exploit this same count
LFU evicts the smallest count; MFU evicts the largest
Counting-based replacement tracks how many times each resident page has been referenced, using that frequency instead of arrival order or recency to pick a victim
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the idea behind Counting-Based replacement. Instead of considering the order or recent usage of pages, this approach uses the reference count as the replacement criterion. The reference count records how many times each resident page has been accessed and increases with every access. Based on this count, LFU (Least Frequently Used) replaces the page that has been accessed the least number of times, whereas MFU (Most Frequently Used) replaces the page that has been accessed the most number of times.

slides.title: LFU Defined
slides.body:
Lowest Count Evicted
Maintains a running reference count per resident frame
Fault victim: page with the minimum count in memory
Ties commonly broken using FIFO or arrival order
Assumes past frequency predicts continuing low future use
LFU replacement evicts the resident page with the smallest reference count, assuming an infrequently used page is least likely to be needed soon
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the LFU (Least Frequently Used) replacement algorithm. It selects the victim page with the smallest reference count, that is, the page that has been accessed the fewest number of times. The operating system maintains a reference count for every resident frame and updates it whenever the page is accessed. If more than one page has the same reference count, the tie is usually broken using FIFO or arrival order. This algorithm works on the assumption that a page with a low past usage frequency is less likely to be needed soon.

slides.title: LFU Key Drawback
slides.body:
New Page Penalised
LFU can wrongly evict a newly loaded page whose count is still small, even though its real usage burst has not yet begun
Recently loaded pages start with a low count
Such pages get evicted before proving their real usage
Pages once heavily used keep a high count indefinitely
High-count pages resist eviction even after their use has stopped
Implementation needs a counter plus a scan for the minimum
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at a major drawback of the LFU algorithm. Since every newly loaded page starts with a low reference count, it may get selected as the victim page before it has a chance to show its actual usage. On the other hand, pages that were heavily used in the past continue to have a high reference count, making them difficult to evict even if they are no longer needed. Also, implementing LFU requires maintaining a counter for each page and scanning to find the page with the minimum reference count, which adds extra overhead

slides.title: MFU Defined
slides.body:
Highest Count Evicted
Fault victim: page with the maximum count in memory
Assumes a low-count page is newer and needed longer
Opposite intuition to both LFU and LRU
Rarely used in practice; mainly a contrasting theoretical policy
MFU replacement evicts the resident page with the largest reference count, reasoning that a heavily used page has likely finished its burst of use
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the MFU (Most Frequently Used) algorithm. Unlike LFU, it selects the victim page with the largest reference count, meaning the page that has been accessed the most number of times. The assumption here is that a page with a low reference count is relatively new and is likely to be needed for a longer time, whereas a heavily used page may have already completed its burst of use. This is the opposite approach to both LFU and LRU, which is why MFU is rarely used in practice and is mainly studied as a theoretical policy.

slides.title: Counting vs Recency
slides.body:
Policy Comparison Table
Counting-based policies use total access frequency, while LRU uses only the most recent access, giving each a different trade-off between accuracy and overhead
tables: Low past freq. = low future need
High past freq. = burst is over

slides.body:
Policy Comparison Table

slides.title: Belady's Anomaly & Practice
slides.body: Belady's Anomaly & Practice
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Belady's Anomaly & Practice

slides.title: Belady's Anomaly Defined
slides.body:
More Frames Worse
Expectation: more frames should reduce or maintain faults
Anomaly: fault count sometimes rises with more frames
First reported by László Bélády in 1969
Occurs only in non-stack algorithms such as FIFO; stack algorithms like LRU and Optimal never exhibit it
Belady's Anomaly is the counter-intuitive result where increasing the number of allocated frames increases the page-fault count for certain replacement algorithms
slides.notes: Now, let's understand Belady's Anomaly. Normally, we expect that increasing the number of Frames will either reduce or at least maintain the number of Page Faults. However, Belady's Anomaly is the unusual situation where adding more Frames actually increases the Page Fault count. This phenomenon was first reported by László Bélády in 1969. It occurs only in non-stack algorithms such as FIFO, whereas stack algorithms like LRU and Optimal never exhibit Belady's Anomaly.

slides.title: Why Anomaly Occurs
slides.body:
FIFO Lacks Property
Ideal behaviour: smaller frame set's pages are a subset of larger set's pages
FIFO's eviction depends only on arrival time, not on this containment
A page dropped with fewer frames may be kept with more, and vice versa
This broken containment is the root cause of the anomaly
A larger frame set should ideally hold every page a smaller frame set holds, but FIFO's arrival-order queue offers no such guarantee
slides.notes: Finally, let's understand why Belady's Anomaly occurs. Ideally, when we increase the number of Frames, the larger Frame Set should contain all the pages present in the smaller Frame Set. However, FIFO does not guarantee this because it makes replacement decisions only based on the arrival order of pages. As a result, a page that is present in memory with fewer Frames may not be present when more Frames are allocated., breaking this containment property. This is the root cause of Belady's Anomaly.

slides.title: Stack Property Explained
slides.body:
Immune Algorithms
Optimal and LRU both satisfy the stack property
FIFO does not guarantee the stack property
LFU and MFU also do not guarantee it in general
Any stack-property algorithm can never suffer Belady's Anomaly
The stack property guarantees that the set of pages held with k frames is always contained within the set held with k+1 frames, ruling out the anomaly
slides.notes: Moving on, let's understand the Stack Property. It states that the pages present with k Frames should always be contained within the pages present with k+1 Frames. Optimal and LRU satisfy this Stack Property, whereas FIFO, LFU, and MFU do not guarantee it. Because of this property, any algorithm that satisfies the Stack Property can never exhibit Belady's Anomaly.
